blocks.text: Software engineer. AI in focus.
I'm Sifen Mekonnen Gebremariam, a software engineer and AI student. From Addis Ababa to Kigali, I carry one question into everything I build: how can this make someone's life better?
From AASTU to Carnegie Mellon University Africa

In June 2026, I graduated in Software Engineering from Addis Ababa Science and Technology University. Today, I'm pursuing a Master of Science in Information Technology at Carnegie Mellon University Africa in Kigali, Rwanda, focusing on artificial intelligence.
Different roots. A shared possibility.

At CMU-Africa, I'm learning alongside people from more than two dozen African countries. We bring different languages, experiences, and ways of seeing the world. Working together is teaching me that our diversity can lead us to ideas none of us would find alone.
Research rooted in African realities.

My research interests include computer vision, machine learning, low-resource African languages, and educational robotics. I am working on Tamashek in Mali with a fellow CMU-Africa student from Mali whom I met in Kigali, alongside Professor Sascha Griffiths. Our aim is to explore how this work could support robots that help in education.

blocks.text: A new chapter, with the same purpose.

In June 2026, I graduated in Software Engineering from Addis Ababa Science and Technology University. That milestone held years of hard work, encouragement from people who believed in me, and a growing sense of responsibility for what I could do with the skills I had gained.

My next chapter brought me from Ethiopia to Kigali, Rwanda, where I'm now pursuing a Master of Science in Information Technology at Carnegie Mellon University Africa, focusing on artificial intelligence. CMU-Africa is the Kigali location of Carnegie Mellon's College of Engineering, part of the U.S. university based in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Here, rigorous study and learning from accomplished professors come together with a purpose close to my heart: preparing people to shape Africa's technological future.
Learning Africa through one another.

Some of my most meaningful learning happens in conversations with classmates. Our community brings together people from more than two dozen African countries, each carrying a different language, history, and understanding of home. A question I see one way can look entirely different to someone beside me.

I'm learning to listen before I propose a solution. I'm learning that unity doesn't ask us to become the same. It asks us to make room for one another. There is beauty in what we bring individually, and possibility in what we can build together.
The person behind the projects.

Long before I wrote code, Taekwondo in Bishoftu taught me patience, discipline, and respect. My father's belief in me still guides the way I approach my education and my work. Those lessons followed me into Technovation at 15, into hackathon teams, and into Se'kela Sustainable Fashion, where we explored how discarded materials could become something people valued.

Building software and working with other young people have taught me that a promising idea is only a beginning. You have to understand who it serves, be willing to hear what isn't working, and keep showing up to improve it.
What I want to help build.

I want to create technology that reflects the lives around us: our languages, our communities, and the realities people face every day. I'm especially curious about how AI can help us build useful, responsible tools that people can trust.

I see Africa as a place of knowledge, creativity, and people with much to contribute. Working on challenges here can lead to ideas that matter far beyond the continent. I want to be part of that work, alongside people who care enough to listen, learn, and build together.

blocks.text: TutForYou: is a mobile platform I built using Flutter and Firebase to seamlessly connect tutors with learners. I implemented features allowing tutors to create detailed profiles, list their subjects, set availability, and manage sessions, while learners can search for tutors based on subject, rating, or location. I integrated real-time chat, session scheduling, and push notifications using Firebase services like Firestore, Authentication, and Cloud Messaging. With a clean, cross-platform interface I developed, TutForYou makes personalized education accessible, reliable, and easy to manage for both tutors and students.

The program mirrors professional industry environments, where diverse expertise is essential to solve complex, multi-faceted problems. Each team works on a single project, applying their specialized knowledge to design, build, and present a functional solution that addresses a societal or environmental need.

We focused on integrating clean energy generation (solar panels and wind turbines) so homes can produce their own power, reducing reliance on external grids and lowering energy costs.

It extends beyond business creation to fostering a mindset of innovation and resilience. This journey is fueled by the belief that the most sustainable ventures are those that generate both economic value and positive social impact.

🔑 Core Philosophies & Growth
This journey has defined my approach to entrepreneurship through key philosophies:
Impact-First Innovation: I start with a pressing problem—like textile waste with Se'kela or food security with Paura Tech—ensuring the venture's purpose is rooted in creating tangible value.
The Builder's Mindset: Programs like ALX Founders Academy equipped me with the rigorous frameworks to de-risk ideas through customer validation, financial modeling, and iterative prototyping.

Leadership as Multiplication: My role with the Hult Prize taught me that the highest leverage for an entrepreneur is to empower others. Success is multiplied by mentoring new founders and strengthening the support ecosystem around them.
This journey is ongoing. It is a commitment to turning observation into action, ideas into ventures, and personal ambition into collective progress.

As the Project Lead for Se’kela Sustainable Fashion , I spearheaded a venture that transformed textile waste into stylish, marketable apparel. This experience was my first deep dive into building a social enterprise from the ground up, blending creative design, sustainable mission, and business strategy to win the LLEA entrepreneurial business idea competition.

Our challenge was clear: address the growing problem of fabric waste in Ethiopia’s fashion industry while creating economic opportunity. My role involved more than just managing a team—it required vision-setting, resourcefulness, and rallying a group around a purpose bigger than any single task.

Se’kela was more than a competition entry—it was a proof of concept for my leadership and entrepreneurial mindset. It confirmed that I thrive when guiding a team from a raw idea to a validated, impactful solution. The experience also sharpened my ability to communicate a vision clearly and persuasively, whether to teammates, mentors, or judges.

Most importantly, Se’kela reinforced my core belief: innovation should solve real problems for real people. This project sits at the heart of my entrepreneurial journey—a tangible example of how I turn observation into action, and ideas into ventures that matter.

I have collaborated with my friends in  creating a small business called Snzro. It is focused on crafting unique, eco-friendly toys and pillows. Its central idea is to create sentimental keepsakes by handcrafting one-of-a-kind items from upcycled materials, thereby giving fabric waste a new life. The brand emphasizes personalization to make each piece a heartfelt gift, combining a commitment to sustainability with detailed, quality craftsmanship.

It functions as a high-impact launchpad, combining practical startup methodologies with real-world mentorship to equip aspiring founders with the skills, mindset, and network needed to build sustainable businesses in Africa and beyond.
My participation in the academy was a deep dive into the systematic mechanics of venture creation.

The Hult Prize is the world's largest engine for the creation and launch of disruptive social good businesses. It challenges university students globally to solve our planet's most pressing issues through innovative, for-good, for-profit startups. Each year, a new theme—such as food security, education, or clean energy—focuses the world's brightest young minds on a single critical challenge, with the winning team receiving $1 million in seed funding.

My involvement with the Hult Prize at Addis Ababa Science and Technology University (AASTU) was a transformative leadership journey. I served as a Campus Mentor, transitioning from being a competitor to empowering the next wave of student innovators.
Physical Fitness: The Discipline of Taekwondo as a Foundational Practice

My approach to physical fitness is not defined by isolated exercise, but by the integrated discipline of Taekwondo—a martial art I have practiced for over a decade, achieving the rank of 2nd Dan Black Belt from the Kukkiwon World Headquarters. This long-term commitment has shaped my understanding of fitness as a holistic system that builds resilience, focus, and character, directly influencing my work in technology and leadership.

Taekwondo taught me that true strength is balanced. It requires not just power in a kick (physical health), but the mental clarity to strategize (absorption), the emotional control to persevere (health), and the respect for an opponent that fosters growth (relationships). This mirrors the SHARP leadership framework I studied, proving that peak performance in any field is a full-spectrum endeavor.

Taekwondo isn't just a sport I practice—it's a discipline that shaped who I am. Earning my 1st Dan Black Belt wasn't about tying a new belt; it was the result of years of sweat, focus, and resilience. Every kick, every poomsae, and every sparring match taught me that progress comes from persistence. Taekwondo gave me mental clarity, physical strength, and the unshakable belief that mastery is a journey, not a destination. I don't just wear the black belt—I live its principles of courtesy, integrity, perseverance, self-control, and indomitable spirit.
I have passed first dan promotion test for Taekwondo on a global level.

I still remember the day I tied on my white belt—clueless but determined. Years later, when my instructor finally wrapped the black belt proceeding to 2nd Dan around my waist, I realized the journey was never about winning trophies. It was about showing up when I was tired, bowing with respect after every loss, and finding calm in chaos. Taekwondo became my meditation, my workout, and my moral compass. The black belt isn't an endpoint—it's a new beginning. And I'm still a student, just with a darker belt.
I have passed the 2 nd DAN Test in a global level for Taekwondo.

The moments that changed how I lead were often simple: a conversation that challenged my assumptions, a teammate finding their voice, or a group of strangers learning to trust one another. Through leadership programs, entrepreneurship, and mentorship, I've learned to pay attention to those moments and to the people behind them.
Make room for one another

During a week at RYLA, people I had only just met began to feel like family. Training, sports, and hiking gave us different ways to connect, and I left with a deeper appreciation for what a community can bring out in each person. I carry that lesson into teams: listen carefully, invite different perspectives, and give people room to contribute in their own way.
Put the learning to work

Aspire pushed me to apply leadership lessons to a project. Safelight brought me closer to the practical work of entrepreneurship, while Civics Unplugged helped me see how individual choices connect to wider community life. Together, these experiences made me more thoughtful about the questions I ask before building: who needs this, whose perspective are we missing, and what would make the idea useful?
Help someone else take the next step

Serving as a Hult Prize Campus Mentor at AASTU gave me a chance to support other student innovators after being a competitor myself. It changed what progress meant to me: helping someone grow in confidence could matter as much as moving my own idea forward. As I continue learning at CMU-Africa, that is the kind of leader I want to become: someone who brings people together and helps good ideas find their way into the world.
I have participated as the first cohort of Light leadership and Entrepreneurship Academy by being Entrepreneurial leader.

I have participated on Rotary Youth Leadership Program that stayed a week long; it was unforgettable moment of time. Starting from spending the week with strangers that became family afterward; it really pushed me to explore who I am, to develop as a leader and see the beauty of being in community. It included from training on various personal growth topics to sports and hiking.

I have participated on a global leadership training program prepared by Harvard Business School. I have learned principles of leadership, worked on a project that pushed me to apply what I have learned and became globally competent in my journey of leadership and entrepreneurship.

blocks.text: Civics Unplugged is a transformative fellowship program dedicated to empowering Generation Z leaders with the tools, community, and vision to build a brighter future for humanity. It moves beyond traditional civic education by creating a dynamic global community of young people committed to active citizenship, innovative problem-solving, and democratic renewal.

My experience as a fellow was a pivotal awakening to my agency within larger societal systems. The program connected my personal drive for impact with the levers of civic engagement, teaching me that leadership extends into community organizing, policy awareness, and collaborative action for the public good. It expanded my perspective from solving discrete technical problems to understanding how to navigate and improve the underlying structures of society.

I am driven by the conviction that technology built in Africa, for Africa, must be built with the entire continent in mind. My journey—from engaging with continental dialogues at events like Africa Celebrates at the UN Economic Commission for Africa to developing blockchain and AI prototypes for local challenges—is guided by this principle. I actively seek to understand shared challenges, from agricultural supply chains to transparent governance, to architect solutions that are locally resonant and broadly relevant.

My participation in the Africa Celebrates event at the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) in Addis Ababa was more than an attendance; it was an immersion into the living, breathing spirit of Pan-Africanism. The event, a vibrant convergence of diplomats, artists, entrepreneurs, and innovators from across the continent, served as a powerful catalyst, transforming my abstract belief in "African solutions for African problems" into a tangible, collective energy.
Presidential Award
Achieving a perfect 4.0 semester GPA
The highest level of academic distinction at the university, reserved for students who demonstrate exemplary mastery across all subjects in a given term.
Dean's Award
Consistent academic excellence and high cumulative performance.
Recognition of sustained scholarly effort, leadership within the faculty, and overall contribution to the academic community.
✨ The Bigger Picture

These are not just awards; they are validators of my disciplined approach and intellectual rigor. Earning a perfect 4.0 GPA, especially in a demanding software engineering curriculum, demonstrates an exceptional capacity for complex problem-solving, meticulous work, and deep understanding.
